prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Mixed · Multilingual glossary (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "English" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 146px
  col 2: header "中文" · longest unbreakable word 14px · one-line width 54px
  col 3: header "日本語" · longest unbreakable word 14px · one-line width 93px
  col 4: header "한국어" · longest unbreakable word 12px · one-line width 64px
  col 5: header "العربية" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 97px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 480px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 479px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 480px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Provide equivalent glossary terms across five languages.","reading":"Readers find a term in one language and scan across its row to compare translations; consistent row alignment helps them keep their place.","groups":["All five columns serve the same role as language equivalents; English can also act as an entry point for readers of this English-language table.","Chinese, Japanese, and Korean terms are compact and can share the middle of the table without requiring identical widths."],"keep_intact":["Individual English and Arabic words and all language names.","Short glossary terms where space permits, especially compact Chinese, Japanese, and Korean entries."],"may_wrap":["Multiword English and Arabic terms can wrap between words.","Longer Japanese and Korean terms may wrap at natural script-appropriate boundaries; wrapping can share row height with translations that already need multiple lines."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[160,65,100,75,79],"idea":"Favor English as the lookup column while giving the three East Asian columns compact widths and allowing longer Arabic terms to wrap."},{"name":"B","widths":[125,70,100,75,109],"idea":"Balance the two outer language columns so longer English phrases and Arabic terms share the wrapping burden."},{"name":"C","widths":[110,65,90,90,124],"idea":"Prioritize Arabic and Korean, accepting more wrapping in English and Japanese to give the other translations room."}]}
